lines.text: A smile in Paris, a wave off Japan, a starry sky over a sleeping village. These are the paintings everyone knows, and the artists who made them.
It begins some seventeen thousand years ago, in a cave in France, where hunters painted horses, stags and bulls across the walls.
Much later in China, a painter unrolled a whole city along one long silk scroll, busy with boats, bridges and crowds.
In Bruges in 1434, Jan van Eyck painted a merchant and a woman in a room so precisely that a tiny mirror reflects the whole scene.
Then came Leonardo da Vinci, painter, engineer and student of nature, whose notebooks are full of flying machines and the human body.
A generation younger, Michelangelo would carve the David, paint the Sistine ceiling and help design the dome of St Peter's.
In Florence, Botticelli painted Venus arriving on a seashell, blown ashore by the winds, one of the first great Renaissance paintings of myth.
Around 1490, Leonardo painted a young woman holding an ermine, turning as if someone had just called her name.
On a monastery wall in Milan, he painted the moment Jesus says one of his friends will betray him. The paint began to flake almost at once.
Meanwhile in the Netherlands, Hieronymus Bosch filled three panels with paradise, pleasure and a nightmare hell, and scholars still argue over what it means.
Around the same time, a picture of Christ was painted that is now given to Leonardo. In 2017 it became the most expensive painting ever sold.
And in Florence, Leonardo began the Mona Lisa, with her soft shading and faint smile. Today she is the most visited painting in the world.
In the Vatican, Raphael gathered the great thinkers of ancient Greece into one grand hall, with Plato and Aristotle at its heart.
Nearby, after four years on his back, Michelangelo finished the Sistine Chapel ceiling, with God reaching out to Adam.
In London, Hans Holbein painted two French envoys, with a strange stretched skull across the floor that only appears when seen from the side.
In Rome, Caravaggio painted saints as ordinary people in sudden light and deep shadow, while his own life ran from trouble to trouble.
In Antwerp, Peter Paul Rubens ran a great workshop of lively Baroque pictures, and found time to work as a diplomat too.
In Amsterdam, Rembrandt mastered light and shadow, painting himself more than eighty times, from bold youth to bankrupt old age.
In quiet Delft, Johannes Vermeer painted rooms lit from a window. He made few pictures and was nearly forgotten for two centuries.
In 1642 Rembrandt painted a militia company stepping out into the light, full of movement, and it became the Netherlands' best-known painting.
In Madrid, Velazquez painted a young princess, her attendants and himself at work, a puzzle of mirrors and viewpoints still debated today.
Around 1665, Vermeer painted a girl in a blue and yellow headscarf glancing over her shoulder, a face no one has ever named.
In Spain, Francisco Goya rose to be court painter, then recorded the horrors of war, and in deafness painted dark visions on his own walls.
In Japan, Katsushika Hokusai spent a long life drawing, and his woodblock prints of Mount Fuji would one day travel the world.
In England, J M W Turner painted skies, seas and light, his later works so loose they seem almost abstract.
Another Japanese printmaker, Hiroshige, showed travellers, rain and snow on the roads of Japan, and his views would inspire European painters.
In 1801, Jacques-Louis David painted Napoleon on a rearing horse in the Alps, a portrait of power made for the ages.
Years later Goya answered with soldiers shooting Spanish civilians in the night, one of the first great paintings against war.
In Germany, Caspar David Friedrich painted a lone man gazing over a sea of fog, the very picture of Romanticism.
In France, Theodore Gericault turned a real shipwreck scandal into a giant canvas of survivors adrift, and Romantic painting was launched.
Across the Channel, John Constable painted a farm cart crossing a stream, a calm picture of the English countryside.
After the revolution of 1830, Delacroix painted Liberty carrying the French flag over the barricades, an image of France ever since.
Around then Hokusai made The Great Wave, curling over tiny boats with Mount Fuji far behind. Copies reached Europe and changed how artists saw.
In Paris, Edgar Degas drew dancers, bathers and racehorses from unusual angles, close to the Impressionists, though he called himself a realist.
In the south of France, Paul Cezanne built pictures from patches of colour and simple shapes. Picasso would call him the father of modern art.
Claude Monet set out to paint light itself, returning to the same haystacks and the same pond again and again.
In India, Raja Ravi Varma painted the gods and epics, and his prints, sold in millions, shaped how a nation imagines them.
Paul Gauguin left banking for painting, worked beside Van Gogh, and later sailed for Tahiti with his bold, flat colours.
Vincent van Gogh made around two thousand works in about ten years, sold almost none, and died at just thirty-seven.
In Vienna, Gustav Klimt led the Secession and covered his paintings in rich golden patterns.
In 1863 Edouard Manet painted Olympia, a nude woman staring straight back at the viewer, and Paris was scandalised.
In Norway, Edvard Munch painted love, illness and death in swirling colour, and his work fed the coming Expressionism.
Born in Russia, Wassily Kandinsky would make some of the first fully abstract paintings, and wrote of colour as if it were music.
Henri Matisse led the Fauves with bold flat colour, and in old age, unable to stand, he painted with scissors and paper.
In 1871 James Whistler painted his mother seated in profile, now one of the best-known American paintings.
In the Netherlands, Piet Mondrian was born, who would paint the world down to black lines and blocks of red, yellow and blue.
In 1872 Monet painted a hazy harbour at dawn. A critic mocked its title, and the insult gave Impressionism its name.
A few years later Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted friends lunching on a balcony over the Seine, full of sunlight and chatter.
Pablo Picasso, born in Spain in 1881, would start Cubism with Georges Braque and change painting more than anyone of his century.
Georges Seurat painted a Sunday in a Paris park entirely in tiny dots of colour that blend in the eye.
In Mexico, Diego Rivera covered public walls with the history of his country and its workers, at home and in the United States.
In America, Georgia O'Keeffe painted giant flowers, skyscrapers and the deserts of New Mexico, and became the mother of American modernism.
In Arles in 1888, Van Gogh painted sunflowers in thick yellow paint, to brighten a room for his friend Gauguin.
A year later, staying in an asylum, he painted a swirling night sky over a quiet village. It is now in New York.
In 1893 Munch painted a figure clutching its face under a blood red sky, and The Scream became the image of modern anxiety.
Then Monet turned to the pond in his garden at Giverny, painting its water lilies some two hundred and fifty times over thirty years.
In 1903 Mark Rothko was born, who would paint huge, glowing fields of colour.
The next year came Salvador Dali, Surrealist, showman and owner of the world's most famous moustache.
In 1907 Picasso painted five women in flat, broken shapes with mask-like faces. Even his friends were shocked, and Cubism was on its way.
That same year in Vienna, Klimt painted The Kiss, a couple wrapped in robes of real gold leaf.
In Mexico, Frida Kahlo was born. After a bus accident in her youth, she painted herself again and again, in pain and in pride.
In America, Jackson Pollock would lay his canvases on the floor and drip and pour paint across them.
Andy Warhol would turn soup cans and film stars into silkscreen prints, asking what art has to do with fame and money.
In Japan, Yayoi Kusama was born, the artist of polka dots, pumpkins and mirrored rooms that seem to go on forever.
In 1929, Rene Magritte painted a pipe and wrote beneath it that this is not a pipe. And of course, it is only a picture.
A year later Grant Wood painted a stern farmer with a pitchfork beside a woman, the most parodied picture of rural America.
In 1931 Dali painted melting pocket watches in a bare dreamscape, and Surrealism had its most famous image.
After the bombing of a Basque town in 1937, Picasso painted Guernica in black, white and grey, a vast cry against war.
That year in England, David Hockney was born, who would paint swimming pools, portraits and bright Yorkshire hills.
In 1939 Kahlo painted two versions of herself side by side, their exposed hearts joined by a single vein.
During the war, Edward Hopper painted a few figures in a bright diner on an empty street at night, a picture of city loneliness.
In New York, Jean-Michel Basquiat was born. He went from graffiti to fame with paintings of words, masks and crowns, and died at twenty-seven.
In 1962 Warhol showed thirty-two canvases of soup cans, one for each flavour, and Pop Art had arrived.
That same year he repeated a photo of Marilyn Monroe fifty times, half in colour and half fading away.
In 1964 Magritte painted a man in a bowler hat with a green apple hiding his face.
From Bristol came Banksy, whose name nobody knows, stencilling rats, children and police on walls around the world.
In 1991 Damien Hirst put a tiger shark in a tank of formaldehyde, the best-known work of the Young British Artists.
And in 2018, seconds after Banksy's Girl with Balloon sold at auction, it shredded itself in its frame, and became a new work.
From a cave wall to a shredded canvas, painting keeps finding new ways to make us stop and look.
